body:
Higher Education in Ancient India

Ancient India had several important centres of higher learning where students studied religion, philosophy, language, medicine, mathematics and other subjects. Taxila, Nalanda, Vallabhi and Vikramashila were among the best-known centres, but they developed in different regions and periods.

These institutions should not be understood as identical to modern universities. Their organisation varied. Some teaching took place under individual scholars, while large Buddhist monasteries developed organised residential arrangements for teachers and students.

A vihara was a Buddhist monastery. A mahavihara was a large monastic establishment that could also function as an important centre of advanced education.

Taxila: Location and Historical Setting

Taxila, also called Takshashila, was situated in the ancient region of Gandhara, in the north-western part of the Indian subcontinent. Its remains are located in present-day Punjab, Pakistan, near Rawalpindi.

Taxila occupied an important position on routes connecting the Indian subcontinent with Central Asia and regions farther west. This location encouraged the movement of merchants, travellers, ideas and students. It was a major centre of learning for several centuries, particularly during the first millennium BCE and the early centuries CE.

Taxila was also an important political and commercial centre. It served as a provincial centre under the Mauryas and later came under other rulers, including the Kushanas. However, its educational reputation cannot be attributed to a single ruling dynasty.

How Teaching Was Organised

Taxila was famous primarily because of its individual teachers and their expertise. Students sought instruction from particular scholars according to the subjects they wished to study.

Teachers generally exercised considerable independence in accepting students, choosing subjects and determining the course of instruction. Discussion, explanation and debate were important teaching methods. Advanced students could also assist in teaching younger students.

It is therefore misleading to imagine Taxila as one centrally administered university with a single founder, a uniform syllabus and departments organised exactly like those of a present-day university.

Subjects and Famous Scholarly Associations

Taxila offered advanced learning in both religious and practical subjects. Its important fields included:

  • Religious and literary studies: ancient scriptures, language, literature and philosophical traditions.
  • Law and administration: rules of conduct, legal learning and matters of governance.
  • Medicine: knowledge relating to diseases, treatment and medical practice.
  • Astronomy: the study of celestial bodies and their movements.
  • Military science: warfare, military skills and related instruction.
  • Arts and crafts: traditional fields of practical and artistic knowledge, including the 18 arts mentioned in educational accounts.

Several distinguished figures are traditionally associated with education at Taxila:

  • Panini: the renowned Sanskrit grammarian associated with the Ashtadhyayi.
  • Jivaka: a celebrated physician in ancient Indian traditions.
  • Chanakya or Kautilya: associated with political thought and statecraft.

These associations are useful for identifying the character of learning at Taxila. They should not be treated as proof that all these figures studied there at the same time or belonged to a single centrally organised institution.

Patronage distinction: Taxila was supported by the wider political and social environment of Gandhara, but its educational development is not securely attributed to one royal founder. This differs from Vikramashila, whose foundation is specifically associated with the Pala ruler Dharmapala.

Why Taxila Matters

Taxila demonstrates that higher education in ancient India could develop through the reputation of teachers and the movement of students across regions. Its strategic location also helped connect intellectual life with wider commercial and cultural exchanges.

Prelims focus

  • Taxila or Takshashila was located in ancient Gandhara, in present-day Pakistan.
  • Its important subjects included scriptures, law, medicine, astronomy and military science.
  • Panini, Jivaka and Chanakya are traditionally associated with Taxila.
  • Taxila was also an important Mauryan provincial centre.
  • Trap: Taxila should not be assigned a single securely established royal founder or confused with a modern centrally administered university.

[Sources: NCERT, It So Happened, Class 8, chapter 'Ancient Education System of India', pp. 69–71, 2024–25 reprint; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, chapters 'Ashoka, the Emperor Who Gave Up War' and 'Traders, Kings and Pilgrims', 2018–19 edition; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Taxila', site description, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Taxila: An Ancient Centre of Learning in North-Western India

body:
Location and Historical Importance

Nalanda Mahavihara was one of the most celebrated centres of higher education in ancient India. It was located in present-day Nalanda district, Bihar, near Rajgir.

Nalanda developed into a large residential centre in which Buddhist monks, teachers and students lived and studied. Its reputation attracted scholars from different parts of India and other Asian countries.

The great institution flourished from approximately the 5th century CE and remained influential for several centuries, extending into the early medieval period.

Foundation and Royal Patronage

Nalanda's early institutional development is generally associated with the Gupta period. The Gupta ruler Kumaragupta I, who ruled in the 5th century CE, is commonly credited with its foundation or early major patronage.

Nalanda continued to receive support after the Gupta period. Important later patrons included:

  • Harshavardhana: the ruler of northern India in the 7th century CE.
  • The Pala rulers: who supported major Buddhist centres of learning in eastern India from the 8th century CE onward.

Royal grants and other donations helped sustain buildings, teachers, students and the daily needs of the monastic community.

Foundation and later patronage are different facts. Kumaragupta I is associated with Nalanda's early foundation, while Harsha and the Palas were important later supporters. They should not all be described as its founders.

Subjects Taught at Nalanda

Nalanda was primarily a Buddhist centre of higher learning, but education there was not confined to Buddhist religious texts.

Its fields of study included:

  • Buddhist philosophy and scriptures: different Buddhist teachings, interpretations and philosophical arguments.
  • Logic: systematic reasoning and methods of examining arguments.
  • Grammar and language: essential for reading, explaining and debating scholarly texts.
  • Vedic studies: knowledge of important non-Buddhist Indian intellectual traditions.
  • Medicine, mathematics and astronomy: scientific and practical subjects.
  • Fine arts, political learning and military knowledge: other subjects mentioned in accounts of the institution's curriculum.

This wide range of subjects is an important distinction. A Buddhist monastic institution could preserve and teach knowledge beyond Buddhist doctrine.

Teaching Methods and Admission

Nalanda was known for learned teachers, organised study and vigorous discussion. Debates helped students clarify ideas, defend arguments and examine competing interpretations.

The Chinese Buddhist traveller Xuanzang studied at Nalanda in the 7th century CE. He described highly accomplished teachers, disciplined monastic life and demanding intellectual discussions.

According to Xuanzang's account, prospective entrants faced difficult questions before admission. This description indicates the importance placed on prior learning and the ability to reason. It should be understood as his account of the institution rather than as a modern admission regulation.

Xuanzang, Yijing and Nalanda

Two Chinese Buddhist monks are especially important for understanding Nalanda:

  • Xuanzang: studied Yogashastra, a body of learning concerning yoga and Buddhist philosophical practice, under the distinguished scholar Shilabhadra.
  • Yijing: also studied at Nalanda and recorded details of Buddhist monastic discipline, education and daily practices.

Their records show that Nalanda formed part of a wider Asian network of Buddhist scholarship. Students travelled long distances to study, obtain manuscripts and carry learned traditions to their home regions.

Prelims focus

  • Nalanda was located in Bihar, near Rajgir.
  • Kumaragupta I of the Gupta dynasty is associated with its early foundation.
  • Harshavardhana and the Pala rulers were important later patrons.
  • Xuanzang studied at Nalanda under Shilabhadra.
  • Xuanzang and Yijing both provide accounts of Nalanda in the 7th century CE.
  • Trap: Nalanda was Buddhist in character but also taught subjects such as grammar, medicine, mathematics and astronomy.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, chapter 'Traders, Kings and Pilgrims', printed pp. 105–106, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, It So Happened, Class 8, chapter 'Ancient Education System of India', pp. 71–73, 2024–25 reprint; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara', Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 18 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, historical description of Nalanda, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Nalanda: A Great Buddhist Residential Centre of Learning

body:
Location: A Centre of Learning in Saurashtra

Vallabhi, also written Valabhi, was an important educational centre in the Saurashtra region of present-day Gujarat. Its ancient site is associated with the area around modern Vallabhipur in Bhavnagar district.

Vallabhi was also the capital of the Maitraka dynasty, which ruled in the region from approximately the 5th to the 8th century CE. Its position as a political and cultural centre helped the growth of learned institutions.

Vallabhi became particularly prominent during the 6th to 8th centuries CE. It was among the important centres of Buddhist learning in western India.

The Maitrakas and Educational Patronage

The growth of education at Vallabhi was closely connected with the patronage of the Maitraka rulers. Their grants supported Buddhist monasteries and other religious and educational establishments.

Merchants and other donors also contributed to educational and religious institutions. Such support helped monasteries provide accommodation and instruction to students.

The Maitrakas are often associated personally with Shaiva religious traditions, but they also made grants to Buddhist monasteries. Thus, a ruler's personal religious affiliation did not necessarily prevent patronage of institutions belonging to another tradition.

Vallabhi was a major centre of learning under the Maitrakas of Gujarat. Its institutional history should be connected with Maitraka patronage rather than with the Gupta or Pala foundation traditions of other universities.

Subjects and Character of Education

Vallabhi developed as a significant centre for advanced Buddhist study and intellectual discussion. Its teaching was associated with several fields:

  • Buddhist religious and philosophical learning: the study and interpretation of Buddhist traditions.
  • Logic: methods of reasoning, argument and scholarly debate.
  • Grammar and literature: the study of language and texts.
  • Law and political learning: subjects relevant to legal understanding and public affairs.

Vallabhi's reputation rested not merely on religious instruction but also on the education of learned people who could participate in debates and public life.

What the Chinese Travellers Recorded

Xuanzang, the Chinese Buddhist monk who travelled through India in the 7th century CE, visited Vallabhi and described its Buddhist establishments.

Yijing, another Chinese Buddhist monk who travelled later in the 7th century, referred to Nalanda and Vallabhi as leading centres of Buddhist learning. His testimony is important evidence of Vallabhi's reputation outside Gujarat.

Travel distinction: Xuanzang is associated with a visit to Vallabhi. Yijing's account recognises Vallabhi's importance, but this reference alone does not establish that he personally visited the city.

Vallabhi and Nalanda: Similarities and Differences

FeatureVallabhiNalanda
Present-day locationGujaratBihar
Major early patronsMaitraka rulersGupta rulers
Later supportMaitrakas and other donorsHarsha and Pala rulers
Educational characterBuddhist learning and other advanced subjectsResidential Buddhist learning and other advanced subjects

Both institutions attracted advanced scholars and supported intellectual discussion. The most useful distinction is their different geographical and political settings: Vallabhi in Maitraka Gujarat and Nalanda in eastern India.

Importance for Gujarat History

Vallabhi demonstrates that Gujarat was an important participant in the educational and intellectual life of early medieval India. Its prominence was linked to the Maitraka political centre, the support of donors and the movement of scholars between regions.

Prelims focus

  • Vallabhi was located in Saurashtra, present-day Gujarat.
  • Its site is associated with modern Vallabhipur in Bhavnagar district.
  • Vallabhi was the capital of the Maitraka dynasty.
  • It was an important centre of Buddhist and other advanced learning.
  • Xuanzang visited Vallabhi; Yijing recognised its importance alongside Nalanda.
  • Trap: Vallabhi is associated with Maitraka patronage, not the Pala ruler Dharmapala.

[Sources: Annette Schmiedchen, 'Maitrakas', Encyclopedia of Ancient History: Asia and Africa, 2021, discussion of Vallabhi, Buddhist endowments and Yijing; H. D. Sankalia, The University of Nalanda, Chapter VIII, discussion of Valabhi; NCERT, It So Happened, Class 8, chapter 'Ancient Education System of India', pp. 69–73, 2024–25 reprint; online sources consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Maitraka grants supported Vallabhi’s Buddhist monasteries, broad higher learning and reputation recorded by Xuanzang and Yijing.
pictures.caption: Vallabhi connected political patronage in Saurashtra with a wider network of Buddhist scholarship.

title: Vallabhi: Gujarat's Major Centre of Early Medieval Education
